newsitem.title: INDIA: India banks mull 0.5-1.0 percentage pt prime cuts.
newsitem.headline: India banks mull 0.5-1.0 percentage pt prime cuts.

text.p: Bankers said on Thursday they expected Indian bank prime lending rates to fall by 50-100 basis points over the next few days following a cut in the bank rate announced by the central bank on Wednesday.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced a one percentage point cut in bank rate, the rate at which banks borrow from the central bank, to 10 percent per annum with immediate effect.
"Prime lending rates will come down as this is a clear signal from the RBI," said K. Kannan, chairman and managing director of state-run Bank of Baroda.
Bankers said a 50-100 basis point cut in prime rates was on the cards.
"I think all banks will now cut lending rates - I see a cut of 0.5-1.0 percentage point," said S. Solomon Raj managing director of private sector IndusInd Bank.
The RBI also announced a one percentage point cut in interest on deposits with maturities from 30 days up to one year and on rupee export credit.
Bankers said individual banks will hold meetings of their boards in the coming days to consider revision of rates.
"We would discuss it in a board meeting before announcing the same," M.G.Bhide, chairman and managing director of state-run Bank of India told Press Trust of India agency.
Bhide also said he expected bank prime rates to come down by 50-100 basis points.
Kannan said Bank of Baroda's management committee will meet on Thursday to consider deposit and lending rate restructuring.
"Banks will have to respond to the RBI's move by cutting lending rates although there is widespread scepticism over whether a cut in rates will boost credit offtake," Kannan said.
Leading banks cut prime rates by 150-200 basis points last year but the impact on credit offtake was negligible.
A slowdown in industrial growth has led to poor credit demand and poor loan disbursals have dogged the banking industry through last year.

The latest RBI statistics show bank loans have grown by only 11.41 billion rupees to 2,776.71 billion over the end-March figure while deposits have risen by 141.12 billion to 5,177.07 billion in the current financial year (April-March).
Growth in industrial output slowed to 8.7 percent in 1996 from 11.6 percent in 1995, according to a Asian Development Bank report released in April.
Kannan said a lowering of rates will be crucial in assisting a revival.
"I think we have seen that many corporate bottomlines have been hit in 1996/97," Kannan said. "I think they will need assistance from banks if they are to pick up."
He however felt that a cut in prime rates might not be the answer.
"Basically, it has little relevance....very few borrowers get funds at prime rates," he said. "We at Bank of Baroda have asked the RBI to let us lend to good borrowers at sub-prime rates."
He said this will help the bank as it did not have to lose revenue by cutting prime rates across the board but only for selected clients.
-- Giri Venkatesan, Bombay newsroom +91-22-265 9000
